seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

msIdentifier.repository: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Yale University

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p: Dear Pound: The day of reckoning being near will you please tell me name and address of the sender of that extra £6?
The news I have to impart is as follows:
Fels : Nothing has been heard or seen of him by me or by anybody else since about the 10 July last.

Mercure : Mmes et M. M. Fontainas , Benda , Barney , Davray, Serruys, Bloch-Savitzky , Monnier , Beach and several others all wrote, spoke, wired and telephoned to Mr Valette Vallette
at intervals concerning me and my novel. But on last Friday at 5.30 p.m (summer time) Mr Valette Vallette , interrogated by Mr Bradley , replied that he had never heard or read a word about me or my book from anybody. Mr Fontainas is reported to have stated to somebody that with a great review like the Mercure (1/4 ½ a page) ce serait très long, très très long .

Lügner(?)-Poe
: The latest I heard is that he has read the play and now, in order to find out what it is about, he is having a mot-à-mot translation made for his own special benefit: viz:
Argument: Jacques, joueur de footbal, achète des œufs dans l’auberge de l’îlot et les mange ensuite avec joie dans un arbre de confitures.

Books: My case of books, papers, documents forwarded by me from Trieste redenta on 29 June last to enable me to write here cannot be found. Several letters and telegrams have been dispatched by several people to several other people. Mlle Serruys’ sister’s husband (of the French Foreign Office) is going to move in the matter.

Quinn : Part of the MS of Ulysses
sent by me to him from Trieste redenta on 10 June 1920 is also lost. He writes that there is no chance of ordinary publication for it, an alliance formed of English imperialists, Irish republicans, Roman Catholics and American presbyterians having been formed to have it seized, the plates sequestrated and publisher and printer imprisoned.

House: A week ago Mr Bloch called and gave me a notice to quit this apartment at the beginning of October. He has let both his flats to other people and is going to live permanently in the country. I am looking for a flat.

Mathers : This gentleman and his wife passing through Paris were kind enough to invite me to a very agreeable dinner in the middle of which appeared Mr Vanderpyl who must have been under the table, I think. He now addresses me as “mon cher Pount”. He asked them if they came from Bloomsbury. They answered yes. On this he embraced me and exclaimed to them –
Mais j’adore ce cher Pount!
I thought you might like to know this.

Bradley: He said that if all cried off perhaps his publisher might consider it. But he has not read what I have written – or am writing – except the play and the stories . He acquired, on my recommendation, I think, the English rights of La Porte Etroite and La Symphonie Pastorale for his house. I dined with him a few times very pleasantly.

Dada: Mr Philippe Soupault asked me to call at his office at a certain hour, between 11.30 and 12. I went three days in succession but never found him. Then he wrote apologizing and asking me to make an appointment by letter. I did so, went and waited three quarters of an hour but he did not come. I wrote then asking had there been some mistake but he did not answer. Is this Dadaism? I ask because in an Irish paper which was sent me lately there was an article about it “founded in Zurich by J.J.”!
Circe : To be continued in my next.
Kind regards to Mrs Pound and yourself. I hope Mr Lewis’s hand is all right again.

postscript.p: P.S. Mr Linati has done a ‘profilo’ of you in the current number of his review.

div.note: JJ is probably referring to an expected payment of interest from a sizable trust that the magazine editor and patron Harriet Shaw Weaver (1876-1961) had settled on him in 1919 and subsequently increased. JJ wrote his brother Stanislaus on 28 October 1920 that “dividend warrants” from this trust had “arrived,” and that he had received from Weaver’s solicitors “a week ago … an extra gift of £200 in the form of a cheque ‘thinking it may be useful at present’” (LIII 26). A grateful JJ had written Weaver on 29 August 1920: “The amount of energy given by me to [Ulysses] has been so great that it has altogether weakened my natural defenses against difficulties and hostilities which would not be slow to take advantage of me but that your generous friendship protects me” (quoted in Mary T. Reynolds, “Joyce and Miss Weaver,” James Joyce Quarterly, vol. 19, no. 4 [Summer 1982]: 385). For further details of the trust that benefited JJ, see JJ to Pound, 24 July 1920, notes; n.d. [September 1920], notes.

Despite being told by Pound that he did not need to repay small sums sent to tide him over, JJ may be referring to a “mysterious £5 cheque” from Pound in early August 1920 (JJ to Pound, 8 August 1920), or to a check for £6 sent by Pound on 10 August. For more details, see JJ to Pound, 13 August 1920, notes; n.d. [1 September 1920], notes.

Florent Fels (1891–1977), French publisher, journalist, and author, had planned to issue a French translation of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man in his journal, Action: Cahiers de philosophie et d’art (LI 120; The Cornell Joyce Collection, 69-70). Candidates for translator were, first, Louis Bagnan (LII 450), then Ludmila Bloch-Savitzky (LI 142), but Fels produced only a review of the novel in Action, no. 6 (December 1920): 63–64. The translation by Savitzky (1881-1957) was published as a book, Dedalus; Portrait de l’artiste jeune par lui-même, by the Paris house, Éditions de La Sirène, in 1924.

JJ had hopes that a French translation of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man would be published serially in the journal Mercure de France, founded and edited by Alfred Vallette (1858-1935), for which the French critic Henry Davray (1873-1944) wrote regularly as a specialist in English literature. JJ wrote Davray on 11 August 1920 that he wanted the Mercure to “arbitrer l’artiste irlandais, jeune homme” (“shelter the Irish artist as a young man”) (LIII 14-15). But on 20 October 1920, JJ reported to Jenny Serruys that the Mercure had given “aucune signe de vie” (“no sign of life”) (LIII 25). Other French journals declined it as well. The French translation of A Portrait had to await publication as a book in 1924 by Ludmila Savitsky. Davray had published a favorable account of JJ’s Exiles and other writings in “Lettres anglaises,” Mercure de France, vol. 121, no. 495 (1 February 1919): 512-18.

André Fontainas (1865-1948), Belgian poet, novelist, critic, and art historian, was a good friend of Ludmila Bloch-Savitzky (1881-1957) and André Spire (1868–1966). Fontainas and his wife met JJ probably in July 1920 at a gathering in Neuilly arranged by Bloch-Savitzky and hosted by Spire (Ellmann, JJ, 488-89). Fontainas’ writings appeared frequently in the journal Mercure de France and in volumes under its publishing imprint. Fontainas and Bloch-Savitzky were well-connected with the Mercure, which JJ hoped would publish a French translation of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man (see Leonid Livak, “‘A Thankless Occupation’: James Joyce and His Translator Ludmila Savitzky,” Joyce Studies Annual [2013]: 36-38, 46-47 & nn. 31, 42, 46; see also notes 3 and 4 above and note 8 below).

Julien Benda (1867-1956), French novelist, philosopher, and cultural critic, whom JJ met during his first weeks in Paris (Ellmann, JJ 489). For a fuller account of Benda, see JJ to Pound, 18 August 1920, notes.

Natalie Clifford Barney (1876-1972), expatriate American playwright, poet, and novelist, was famous for her Latin Quarter literary salon. Pound, who was a good friend of Barney’s, facilitated JJ’s contact with her soon after JJ’s arrival in Paris (for further details, see JJ to Pound, 18 August 1920, notes).

JJ was eager to have his play Exiles and his novel A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man translated into French, to bolster his standing in Paris. Jenny Serruys (1886-1983), a French literary figure, was an early candidate for translating A Portrait, but she did not do so. (Ludmila Bloch-Savitsky [1881-1957], another new acquaintance of JJ’s, published a French translation of A Portrait in 1924.) Much later, Serruys did produce a French translation of Exiles (Les Exilés) which was published under her married name J.S. Bradley by nrf Gallimard in Paris in 1950. (For more on Serruys and Bloch-Savitsky, see notes 4-5 above; JJ to Pound, 24 July 1920, notes.)

Adrienne Monnier (1892-1955), French writer and publisher, owned a bookshop and lending library, La Maison des Amis des Livres, at 7 rue de l’Odéon, Paris. Across the street, her companion Sylvia Beach (1887-1962) later located her English language bookshop, Shakespeare and Company, which served as publisher of the first edition of JJ’s Ulysses in 1922. JJ met Monnier and Beach in July 1920 at a gathering in Neuilly arranged by Ludmila Bloch-Savitzky and hosted by the French poet and critic André Spire (Ellmann, JJ, 488-89).

William Aspenwall Bradley (1878-1939) was an American writer and critic and the fiancé of Jenny Serruys. Together they assisted JJ in various ways during his first months in Paris (see JJ to Pound, 24 July 1920, notes; n.d. [1 September 1920], notes).

These numbers may refer to page or font size of the Mercure de France or to some sort of payment per page for authors. Numbers of the Mercure had two parts: “[t]he first half … contains essays, presumably the best in Europe, [and] also prose fictions and poems. The second half contains the ‘Review of the fortnight’ [with] reviews of french novels, french books of history or criticism, french drama, summary of other french magazines, journals etc. Then come sections on English, German, Russian, Spanish, italian, American, etc etc, books. A section on art. etc. Thus you have a two fold magazine, one part creative & one part critical” (The Selected Letters of Ezra Pound to John Quinn, 1915-1924, ed. Timothy Materer [Durham, NC: Duke University Press, 1991], 32-33). The pages devoted to creative writing were printed with larger typeface and more interlineal leading than were pages of the critical section. Serialized in the Mercure, A Portrait might have run to eight or ten installments of some thirty pages each.
Fr. “It would be very, very long,” or “would take a very, very long time” – that is, the serial publication of A Portrait in the Mercure de France. This plan was never realized.
“Lügner” is the German term for liar. JJ may be expressing his annoyance at Lugné-Poe’s toying with Exiles but failing to produce the play.

Aurélien-Marie Lugné (1869-1940), known as Lugné-Poë, was a French actor and theater director who was considering a Paris production of JJ’s play Exiles. In June 1921, however, he concluded that staging Exiles would lose money (Ellmann, JJ 497-98). For a fuller account, see JJ to Pound, 18 August 1920, notes.

Loose translation: “James, a football [or soccer] player, buys some eggs at the inn of the isle and then eats them with delight in a tree of jam preserves.” Lugné-Poë had had a “mot-à-mot” (word for word or verbatim) translation made of JJ’s Exiles (see JJ to Pound, 16 November 1920). JJ pretends here that this translation has yielded a summary (or argument) of the play based on a crude, phonetic rendering of its title page, “Exiles: A Play in Three Acts by James Joyce.” The whimsical conversions from English to French include JJ’s name: “James” becomes “confiture, Jacques” (“confiture” meaning “jam”); and “Joyce” becomes “la joie” (JJ liked to point out that “Joyce” and “Freud” both meant “joy” or “delight” [see Ellmann, JJ 490]).

JJ uses the phrase “Trieste redenta” (Trieste redeemed or freed from Austro-Hungarian rule after its annexation by Italy following the war) as a mocking tribute to a city that he believed had been more efficient and pleasanter to live in before the war, when pro-Italian Irredentism was an aspiration rather than a reality.

JJ sent a case of books and papers from Trieste on 29 June 1920 for his use in Paris (“to enable me to write”). It was finally delivered to him on the evening of 27 October 1920 (LIII 23, 26). For more details, see JJ to Pound, n.d. [1 September 1920], notes.

The New York lawyer John Quinn (1870-1924), a collector of modern art and literary manuscripts, was paying for the Ulysses manuscript in installments, and had sent 3,400 francs or $250 on 15 August 1920 (Myron Schwartzman, “‘Quinnigan’s Quake!’ John Quinn’s Letters to James Joyce, 1916-1920,” Bulletin of Research in the Humanities, vol. 81, no. 2 [Summer 1978]: 237, 241-42, 245-46, 254, 258). JJ wrote Quinn on 2 September 1920 that the 15 August payment had arrived (LI 145). There was some confusion at this time because a portion of the manuscript sent by JJ in June 1920 from Trieste had not yet reached Quinn (see LI 145; LIII 21-22). Quinn acknowledged receipt of the missing portion, however, on 27 September 1920; at that point he had “received altogether fourteen episodes of ‘Ulysses,’ beginning with ‘Telemachus’ and ending with ‘Oxen of the Sun’” (Schwartzman 253). For additional details, see JJ to Pound, 24 July 1917, notes; n.d. [1 September 1920], notes.

Because of the active anti-obscenity movement in America at this time, Quinn was urging JJ to consider a private edition of Ulysses, to be published by B.W. Huebsch of New York if possible, limited to 1,000 or 1,250 copies selling for $8 or $10 each (Quinn to JJ, 15 August 1920, John Quinn Memorial Collection, Manuscripts & Archives Division, New York Public Library; for more details, see JJ to Pound n.d. [1 September 1920], notes). Ulysses had been appearing serially in the New York magazine The Little Review since March 1918. What JJ does not yet seem to know, despite his prophetic remarks here, is that the New York Society for the Suppression of Vice was about to file, in the coming days, an official complaint against the July-August 1920 number of The Little Review, which contained the portion of the “Nausicaa” episode in which Leopold Bloom masturbates at the seashore (see Paul Vanderham, James Joyce and Censorship: The Trials of Ulysses [London: Macmillan, 1998], 41-42).

The Russian-born Ludmila Bloch-Savitsky (1881-1957) and her husband, a railroad chief engineer named Marcel Bloch (1881-1951), had allowed JJ and family to have their flat, rent-free, for their first three months in Paris.

JJ wrote Pound on 5 November 1920 that after an “entire month of flathunting,” he and his family were back at 9 rue de l’Université, the private hotel they had stayed at when they first arrived in Paris in July 1920 (LIII 27).

note.p: Most likely Edward (“Bill”) Powys Mathers (1892-1939), an English poet who translated and compiled much Asian, Arabic, and Persian prose and poetry. His publications included what he believed to be “the first general English anthology of Asiatic verse,” Coloured Stars: Versions of Fifty Asiatic Love Poems (Oxford: B.H. Blackwell, 1919); Black Marigolds (Oxford: B.H. Blackwell, 1919), a “free interpretation” of a love poem by the 11th-century Kashmiri poet Kavi Bilhana; and The Garden of Bright Waters: One Hundred and Twenty Asiatic Love Poems (Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 1920). His translations of “Five Afghan Love Poems” were printed – between translations of work by Remy de Gourmont and Julien Benda – in The Dial, vol. 69, no. 4 (October 1920): 372-76. Mathers compiled and published adaptations of J.C. Mardrus’s French translation of The Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, privately printed in London by John Rodker in 1923 for subscribers of the Casanova Society. His multivolume collection of translations of Asian folktales, The Eastern Anthology, was published by Rodker in London in 1927. As “Torquemada,” Mathers composed tormenting crossword puzzles for the London Observer from 1926 until his death. In his ABC of Reading (1934; rpt. New York: New Directions, 1960), Pound included literary “exhibits” for “any reader of sufficient intelligence [wanting] as good a game as Torquemada’s cross-word abominations” (95). In 1926-1927, Mathers would be a victim, like JJ, of the lawful piracies Samuel Roth, who reprinted Mathers’ rather racy translations from the Arabic in his New York magazine, Two Worlds Monthly.

Mathers’ spouse was Rosamond Crowdy (1886-1965), whom he married in 1919. She was a translator of French authors, including Restif de La Bretonne and Théophile Gautier. After Pound had been deemed unfit to stand trial for treason in 1946 and placed in a mental hospital in Washington, DC, Rosamond wrote kindly to him, recalling the early days in London when Pound would appear with “flaunting hair and beard and velvet jacket,” and adding that “Bill never forgot your generosity and value as his critic” (Ezra and Dorothy Pound: Letters in Captivity, 1945-1946, ed. Omar Pound and Robert Spoo [New York: Oxford University Press, 1999], 340-41).

The likelihood that Bill and Rosamond Mathers were JJ’s dinner companions in Paris is strengthened by Pound’s remark to his mother on 7 October 1920: “Mathers back from France” (Ezra Pound to His Parents: Letters 1895-1929, ed. Mary de Rachewiltz et al. [Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2010], 472).

div.note: Fritz-René Vanderpyl (1876-1965), Belgian (often described as Dutch) novelist, poet, gastronome, and art critic for Le Petit Parisien. Though he was a bit overwhelmed by Vanderpyl’s boisterous conversation and personality, JJ liked him and spent time with him in Paris (for more details, see JJ to Pound, 18 August 1920; n.d. 1 September 1920, notes).
Fr. “But I adore this dear Pound!” Vanderpyl sometimes called JJ “Pount” (see also JJ to Pound, n.d. [1 September 1920]).

William Aspenwall Bradley (1878-1939) was an American writer and critic and the fiancé of Jenny Serruys, who later translated JJ’s play Exiles into French. Together they assisted JJ in various ways during his first months in Paris (see JJ to Pound, 24 July 1920, notes). Bradley was a scout for Harcourt, Brace and Co.; around 1923, Bradley and Serruys established the William A. Bradley Literary Agency in Paris, which represented important authors on both sides of the Atlantic, including André Gide. They helped Gertrude Stein place The Autobiography of Alice B. Toklas (1933) and The Making of Americans (1934) with Harcourt (Cécile Cottenet, Literary Agents in the Transatlantic Book Trade: American Fiction, French Rights, and the Hoffman Agency [London: Routledge, 2017], n.p.).

JJ’s play Exiles, published simultaneously by Grant Richards in London and B.W. Huebsch in New York in 1918; and his collection of short stories, Dubliners, first published by Grant Richards in London in 1914.

André Gide’s 1909 novel La Porte étroite depicts the intense, unresolved emotional relationship of cousins, Jerome and Alissa, in a French coastal town. It was translated into English by Dorothy Bussy as Strait is the Gate and published in London by Jarrolds and in New York by Alfred A. Knopf in 1924. La Symphonie pastorale was translated into English as The Pastoral Symphony by Thurston Macauley and published in Great Short Novels of the World, ed. Barrett H. Clark (London: Heinemann; New York: Robert M. McBride, 1927).

Philippe Soupault (1897-1990), French poet, novelist, and critic, was active in Dadaism and later helped found the Surrealist movement with André Breton. At the time he met JJ, Soupault was coediting the magazine Littérature with Breton and Louis Aragon, and working on translations of William Blake, whom he considered a forerunner of Surrealism. Soupault was one of a group of persons recruited to produce a French translation of Anna Livia Plurabelle (published in 1931 in La Nouvelle Revue Française as “Anna Livie Plurabelle”), and he became a friend of JJ and his family. For more details concerning Soupault, see JJ to Pound, 26 September 1930, notes.

On 14 September 1920, JJ asked his brother Stanislaus to contradict the report that “I founded in Zurich the dadaist movement which is now exciting Paris (report of Irish press last week)” (LIII 22). JJ’s proximity to Dadaism in Zurich is explored wittily and imaginatively in Tom Stoppard’s play Travesties (premiered in 1974).

JJ was working at this time on “Circe,” the fifteenth and longest episode of Ulysses. He announced to Pound in a Christmas card dated 20 December 1920 that “Circe” was “finished this morning at last” (LIII 34). (For a fuller account of “Circe,” see JJ to Pound, 5 June 1920, notes.)

During their holiday together in France in August 1920, T.S. Eliot and Wyndham Lewis rented bicycles for getting about. The handlebars fell off Lewis’s machine, throwing him to the ground and causing him to injure his hand. He worried that he had contracted lockjaw from the wound (Peter Ackroyd, T.S. Eliot: A Life [New York: Simon & Schuster, 1984], 102; see also JJ to Pound, n.d. [1 September 1920], notes).

The Milan review Poesia, edited by Mario Dessy (1902-1979), printed, in volume 1, number 5-6 (August-September 1920): 11-17, an essay titled “Ezra Pound” by the Italian writer and translator, Carlo Linati (1878–1949), along with a bibliography, several of Pound’s poems, and a photograph of Henri Gaudier-Brzeska’s sculpture of Pound’s head. For a fuller account of JJ, Pound, and Poesia, see JJ to Pound, 18 May 1920, notes.
